pedagogy.summary: Dividing a quantity in a given ratio is the formal KS3 procedure: for a ratio a:b (or a:b:c), the TOTAL number of parts is a+b(+c); one part = quantity ÷ total parts; each share = its parts × one part. Two things distinguish this from earlier unequal-sharing work: it extends cleanly to THREE-part ratios (divide 180 in 1:2:3), and it goes both ways — pupils must also express a completed division back AS a ratio in simplest form (10 and 14 becomes 5:7), and read off a part as a fraction of the whole. The persistent hazard is using a part rather than the SUM of parts as the denominator; the fix is the same find-one-part routine, kept visible on a bar model.
bestPractices: Standardise the routine explicitly: total parts = sum of all ratio numbers → one part = quantity ÷ total → multiply each ratio number by one part.
Extend to three-part ratios immediately (1:2:3 → 6 parts) so the 'sum ALL the parts' step is generalised, not tied to two shares.
Practise the reverse direction: given the actual shares, write them as a ratio and simplify (10:14 → 5:7), and state a share as a fraction of the whole.
Keep the bar model as the check: the number of equal segments equals the sum of the ratio numbers; adding the shares must return the original quantity.
Distinguish part-to-part (a:b) from part-to-whole (a out of a+b) in the notation, since the same numbers appear in both.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / tape diagram with a+b(+c) equal segments
Ratio table (parts | value) extended to three columns for three-part ratios
Simplest-form ratio from actual shares (divide by the HCF)
commonMisconceptions: Dividing by a single part rather than the sum of parts (÷3 or ÷5 instead of ÷8), or in a 3-part ratio forgetting to include every part in the total.
Sharing the quantity equally among the number of terms (180 into three equal 60s for 1:2:3).
When reversing, writing the shares as a ratio without simplifying (10:14 left un-reduced), or reversing the order.
Confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole — stating a share as a/b of the whole rather than a/(a+b).

learn.summary: Divide a quantity in a given ratio using the find-one-part routine: total parts = sum of ALL ratio numbers; one part = quantity ÷ total parts; each share = its ratio number × one part. The guidance generalises this to three-part ratios (divide 180 in 1:2:3 = 6 parts, not 3) and works both directions: express a completed division back as a simplest-form ratio (10 and 14 → 5:7) and state a share as a fraction of the whole. The persistent hazard is using one part, rather than the sum of parts, as the denominator; a bar/tape model with the correct number of equal segments keeps the correct total visible as a check.

activities.title: Ratio-divider on a tape diagram (forward direction)
feedback: If the strip is cut into three segments for 1:2:3, flag it: count that 1+2+3 = 6 segments are needed before the fill unlocks.

If the learner divides by the number of ratio terms or by a single term instead of the sum of parts (e.g. 180 ÷ 3 = 60) or shares equally (60, 60, 60), show the six-segment bar and recompute one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
If the learner finds one part but stops (answers '30', or '1, 2, 3'), prompt that 30 is only ONE part: ask how many parts each share has, then multiply (1×30, 2×30, 3×30 → 30, 60, 90).
If the shares don't sum to the original quantity, prompt a recount of segments — the total must return 180.
activities.rationale: An optional interactive tape diagram that refuses an incorrect number of segments can make the '÷ total parts' step explicit and give immediate feedback; because the learner segments and fills the bar, the task lets them produce the working rather than only recognise a finished answer. The refusal mechanism is one illustrative design, proposed rather than required or uniquely effective, and its efficacy is not source-verified; it teaches the National Curriculum objective of dividing a quantity in a given ratio.
sourceClaims: Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
learnerActions: Enter a ratio such as 1:2:3 and cut the strip into the SUM of the parts — six equal segments for 1:2:3, not three.
Let the quantity (e.g. 180) distribute across the equal segments and read off one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
Colour 1, 2 and 3 adjacent segments to read the shares 30, 60 and 90, then add them to check they return 180.
Repeat with a two-part ratio (e.g. share £60 in 2:3: 5 parts, one part = 12, shares 24 and 36, summing to 60).
activities.intendedInsight: A three-part ratio 1:2:3 needs six equal parts, not three; dividing once by the total number of parts and then scaling each term is the whole routine, and the shares must add back to the original quantity.

activities.title: Reverse station: write shares as a simplest-form ratio
feedback: If the learner leaves 10:14 un-simplified, prompt: what common factor divides both? Divide by 2 to get 5:7.
If the order is reversed to 14:10, point back to which share came first (10) and restore the matching order.
activities.rationale: The forward division task does not test simplification, so a separate reverse task is needed to secure it. Casting simplification as dividing both terms by the HCF connects to prior fraction work.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Take two actual shares (e.g. 24 sweets shared as 10 and 14) and write them as a ratio 10:14.
Simplify by dividing both terms by their highest common factor (÷2) to reach 5:7, keeping the order matching the shares as stated.
Explain how this is like simplifying a fraction, and check you have not reversed the order (14:10 is wrong for 10 then 14).
activities.intendedInsight: A completed division can be expressed back as a ratio, and a ratio must be reduced to simplest form by dividing by the common factor — directly analogous to simplifying a fraction.

activities.title: Part of the whole as a fraction
feedback: If a learner writes the middle share of 1:2:3 as 2/3, point to the six segments: the denominator is the total parts, so it is 2/6 = 1/3.
Compare 2/6 and 2/3 side by side so the distinction between part-to-part and part-to-whole is visible.
activities.rationale: Confusing a:b with a/b of the whole is a documented classic error; anchoring the denominator to the counted total parts on the bar addresses it directly.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
learnerActions: For 1:2:3, state what fraction of the whole each share is: 1/6, 2/6 (=1/3) and 3/6 (=1/2), using the TOTAL of 6 parts as the denominator.
Contrast part-to-part with part-to-whole explicitly: the middle share is 2 parts out of 6 total, so 2/6, NOT 2/3.
Optionally toggle a colour band to light each part and reveal its fraction of the whole.
activities.intendedInsight: When stating a share as a fraction of the whole, the denominator is the SUM of all parts (a+b+c), not another single term; part-to-part and part-to-whole use the same numbers differently.

activities.title: Checks for understanding (written/selected response)
feedback: For 60, 60, 60: that divides equally rather than in 1:2:3 — re-form the total of 6 parts and scale each term.
For 10:14 chosen as final: it is not yet simplified — divide both terms by 2 to reach 5:7.
For 2/3: the denominator should be the total of 6 parts, giving 2/6 = 1/3.
activities.rationale: Selected/short responses efficiently reveal the equal-share and un-simplified-ratio errors, but they confirm recognition and recall rather than requiring the learner to build the segmented bar and produce the working; use alongside the construction tasks.
learnerActions: Fill in: divide 180 in 1:2:3 → __, __, __ (answer 30, 60, 90; the equal-share response 60, 60, 60 is a common error).
Choose the simplest-form ratio for shares of 10 and 14 (answer 5:7; the un-simplified 10:14 is a distractor).
State what fraction of the whole the middle share of 1:2:3 is (answer 2/6 = 1/3).
activities.intendedInsight: Three-part division, reverse-to-ratio, and part-of-whole can each be checked, with 'shared equally' and 'un-simplified ratio' as the diagnostic error responses; add a two-part item (e.g. £60 in 2:3) if two-part division is also to be checked.

constraints: Treat the forward division and the reverse (shares → simplest-form ratio) as distinct objectives: the forward task does not exercise simplification, so include a separate reverse task.

A static segmented reference bar (e.g. six equal segments for 1:2:3) with tap-to-reveal 'one part = total ÷ sum of parts' can consolidate the routine but does not let the learner segment, fill, or reverse a division themselves — it is a reference card, not a substitute for construction.
Selected-response checks confirm recognition/recall; they do not require the learner to build the bar or produce the working, so pair them with construction tasks for full evidence.
Always re-include every term in the total: a three-part ratio must sum all parts (1+2+3 = 6), and the shares must add back to the original quantity as a check.
Keep part-to-part (a:b) and part-to-whole (a out of a+b+c) distinct in notation, since the same numbers appear in both.
After finding one part, scale each term (×1, ×2, ×3) — reporting one part alone, or '1, 2, 3', is incomplete.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic checked): 180 ÷ 6 = 30; shares 30+60+90 = 180 ✓. £60 in 2:3 → 5 parts, 60 ÷ 5 = 12, shares 24 and 36, sum 60 ✓. 10:14 ÷2 = 5:7 ✓. Middle share of 1:2:3 = 2/6 = 1/3 ✓; largest share 3/6 = 1/2 ✓.

The legacy entry asserted a dividing procedure 'gains nothing' from dialogue and that 3D 'adds nothing' because partitioning is one-dimensional. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been dropped rather than propagated as universal laws; the tape/bar model is retained as a well-fitted representation without claiming other media cannot teach this.
The 'refusal to cut into three segments' is preserved as one optional, illustrative feedback mechanism, not a mandatory or uniquely effective design; its efficacy is untested.

Restored the original assessment's 'performance' error pattern (finds one part but forgets to multiply each term back) as explicit feedback in the forward-division activity, as it was missing from the source candidate.

The original probeDeeper listed '3/3, 3/6, or 3/1' as candidate answers for the largest share; only the correct 3/6 = 1/2 is used, and the erroneous options were not migrated as learner-facing choices.

probeDeeper: How many equal parts are there altogether in 1:2:3? Why 6 and not 3?
Add your three amounts together — do they make 180? What would it mean if they didn't?
What fraction of the whole 180 is the largest share? (counterexample: is it 3/3, 3/6, or 3/1 — and why?)
For 10:14, how did you get 5:7 — what did you divide by, and how is that like simplifying a fraction?
assess.correctAnswer: For 180 in 1:2:3: total parts = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30; the shares are 30, 60 and 90 (which add to 180). For the reverse: 10:14 simplifies (÷2) to 5:7.

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by a single part or by the number of terms rather than the SUM of all parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the bar cut into 1+2+3 = 6 equal segments and count them; one part = 180 ÷ 6. Check the shares add back to 180. Reteach ratio notation and the total-parts idea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 180 ÷ 3 = 60 and gives 60, 60, 60 (equal), or 180 ÷ 1 / ÷2 / ÷3 separately; total parts of 6 never formed

errorPatterns.pattern: When reversing, writes the shares as a ratio without simplifying (or reverses the order)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat it like simplifying a fraction: divide both by the common factor (2). Keep the order matching the shares as stated. Reteach ratio simplification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 10:14 as the final answer, or writes 14:10, not dividing by the HCF to 5:7

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses part-to-part with part-to-whole — states a share as a/b of the whole rather than a/(a+b+c)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the six segments: the denominator is the TOTAL parts. Contrast 2/6 with 2/3 explicitly. Reteach the vocabulary of part-to-part vs part-to-whole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up, says the middle share of 1:2:3 is 2/3 of the whole rather than 2/6 = 1/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds one part correctly but forgets to multiply each term back
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'that's ONE part — how many parts does each share have?' Prompt the multiply and the add-back check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 180 ÷ 6 = 30 and answers '30' or '1, 2, 3' rather than 30, 60, 90

responseLevels.gap: Shares equally (60,60,60) or divides by one part; cannot form the total of 6 parts, and leaves a reversed ratio un-simplified.
responseLevels.full: Sums all parts to 6, finds one part = 30, gives 30/60/90 checked to 180, simplifies 10:14 to 5:7, and correctly states a share as its fraction of the whole (e.g. 2/6 = 1/3) — handling both directions and three-part ratios.
responseLevels.partial: Divides 180 correctly via 6 parts to 30/60/90, but leaves 10:14 un-simplified, or states a share as part-of-part not part-of-whole — the reverse direction or the fraction interpretation is not yet secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Divide 180 in the ratio 1:2:3. Work out the three amounts, and show your working. Then, separately: 24 sweets were shared as 10 and 14 — write that sharing as a ratio in its simplest form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who has the routine sums all three parts to 6, divides once, and scales — shares total 180. A pupil dividing by the number of terms shares equally (60, 60, 60) or divides by one part; a pupil who cannot reverse leaves 10:14 un-simplified. Watching the working shows exactly which step fails, and the reverse task separately tests simplification, which the forward task does not.
